items.title: The Orange Book: Management of Risk, Principles and Concepts
items.publisher: HM Treasury and Government Finance Function
items.locator: Section D, paragraphs D6 to D8, p.23 (PDF page 25)
items.quote: retaining the risk by informed decision
items.why: Source of the quotation. The UK government's risk standard, written for central government and widely borrowed. D6 lists the options: avoid, take or increase, retain by informed decision, change likelihood, change consequences, share (for example through commercial contracts). D8 asks for the rationale, the proposed actions, those accountable and responsible for approving and implementing, resources, performance measures and dates. The words tolerate, treat, transfer and terminate do not appear in this edition. Not binding on companies.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Table 4, MANAGE 1.2 to 1.4, p.32 (PDF page 37); section 1.2.3, p.8
items.quote: Treatment of documented AI risks is prioritized based on impact, likelihood, and available resources or methods.
items.why: International comparator, voluntary. MANAGE 1.3 names the response options as mitigating, transferring, avoiding or accepting, and asks that responses to high-priority risks be planned and documented; MANAGE 1.4 asks that residual risks to downstream acquirers and end users be documented. US framework with no legal force in the UK.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 9: Risk management system
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: the overall residual risk of the high-risk AI systems is judged to be acceptable
items.why: The only binding text read that sets a test for acceptance: residual risk per hazard and overall must be judged acceptable, after elimination or reduction by design, then mitigation and control, then information and training for deployers. A provider duty for high-risk systems, not a deployer duty. Article 9 itself is not marked amended. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text; the page states it is based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026 and marks Digital Omnibus changes NEW or AMENDED. EU law; not UK law.

items.title: Data protection impact assessments: How do we do a DPIA?
items.locator: Sections 'Step 6: How do we identify mitigating measures?' and 'Step 7: How do we conclude our DPIA?'
items.quote: whether each risk has been eliminated, reduced, or accepted
items.why: The regulator's version of a treatment decision. For each risk record whether it is eliminated, reduced or accepted, the residual risk, and who approved; document the data protection officer's advice and the reasons if it is not followed. 'You do not always have to eliminate every risk', but an accepted high risk must go to the regulator before processing. The page carries the notice that the guidance is under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act. No date printed; page metadata gives 18 February 2026.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 36: Prior consultation
items.quote: would result in a high risk in the absence of measures taken by the controller to mitigate the risk
items.why: The binding limit on acceptance where personal data is involved: a high risk that is not mitigated cannot simply be accepted in-house; the controller must consult the regulator first. The text reads 'the Commission' from 30 September 2026.

items.title: Equality Act 2010, section 109: Liability of employers and principals
items.quote: Anything done by an agent for a principal, with the authority of the principal, must be treated as also done by the principal.
items.why: Why contractual transfer has limits. Acts of employees and of agents acting with authority are treated as the organisation's own, whether or not it knew or approved. Whether a software supplier is an 'agent' for this purpose has not been decided in any case read; the brief says so. England, Wales and Scotland.

items.title: Equality Act 2010, section 144: Contracting out
items.quote: A term of a contract is unenforceable by a person in whose favour it would operate
items.why: A contract term cannot exclude or limit the Act. This stops an organisation contracting out of its duties to the people affected; it does not stop a supplier agreeing to indemnify the organisation for the cost. That distinction is the accurate form of the legacy claim.

items.title: Understanding artificial intelligence risk in insurance products: the challenges
items.locator: Paragraphs under 'What is AI?' and 'Protective effects and risk mitigation' (final paragraph)
items.quote: depending on whether the clause in use affirms coverage, applies a sub-limit or excludes the risk entirely
items.why: Insurance as a route for transfer, from the market body itself. The association treats AI as software and so as a subset of cyber risk under its model cyber clauses; whether a loss is covered depends on the clause used. No dedicated model AI exclusion or affirmative AI clause was found on the association's site in this pass. Article by its head of technical underwriting; not a regulator.

items.title: Understanding AI Exposures: AI Loss Scenarios Survey Results
items.locator: Executive summary, 'Are insureds managing the risks (of AI errors causing insured losses) adequately?'; 'Methodology' (144 responses)
items.quote: Only 18% of global responses suggested that insureds’ existing AI risk management/safety procedures are inadequate.
items.why: Source of the figure. Opinion survey of Lloyd's market members: 144 responses collected in Q2 and Q3 2025, 94% from underwriters. It measured confidence, not claims: the report says it 'did not collect risk management data, claims information or data from external sources', and it declined to report findings on exclusions. No date printed on the page.

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: What are the accountability and governance implications of AI?
items.locator: Section 'How do we identify mitigating measures?', final paragraph; section on outsourcing and third-party AI systems, final paragraph
items.quote: the DPIA should document the residual levels of risk posed by the processing
items.why: Applies treatment and residual risk to AI specifically, and says an organisation should be able to modify a bought-in service or switch provider if it stops being compliant. The page carries the notice that the guidance is under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act.

items.title: Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977, section 2: Negligence liability
items.quote: In the case of other loss or damage, a person cannot so exclude or restrict his liability for negligence
items.why: A binding limit on moving risk by contract. Liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence cannot be excluded at all; for other loss a term or notice excluding or restricting liability for negligence stands only so far as it is reasonable. It cuts both ways: it limits what an organisation can push on to others and what a supplier can disclaim. General contract law, not written for AI; s.2 does not apply to consumer contracts (Consumer Rights Act 2015 instead). England, Wales and Northern Ireland; Scotland has its own Part.

items.title: SS2/21: Outsourcing and third party risk management (November 2024 update)
items.publisher: Prudential Regulation Authority, Bank of England
items.quote: Boards and senior management, in particular individuals performing SMFs, cannot outsource their responsibilities.
items.why: A UK regulator's statement that sharing a risk with a supplier does not move accountability: the firm stays fully accountable for its regulatory obligations. The same chapter expects a documented exit plan for material arrangements. Applies to PRA-regulated banks, insurers and designated investment firms only; a supervisory statement, not a rule.

items.title: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024
items.quote: any material controls which have not operated effectively as at the balance sheet date, the action taken, or proposed, to improve them
items.why: The code-level expectation that treatment is checked and reported, not only decided: the board reviews the effectiveness of risk management and internal control at least annually, declares whether material controls were effective, and describes those that were not and the action taken. Provision 28 asks how principal risks are being managed or mitigated. Applies on a comply-or-explain basis to listed companies; Provision 29 applies to accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2026. Not about AI specifically.

items.title: Risk Management in the Artificial Intelligence Act
items.publisher: European Journal of Risk Regulation (Cambridge University Press); author Jonas Schuett
items.locator: Section V.2 'Risk management process, Article 9(2)', paragraph following Footnote 106
items.quote: If it turns out that it is not possible to reduce residual risks to an acceptable level, the development and deployment process must be stopped.
items.why: Peer-reviewed, open-access legal analysis of the EU risk management duty: assess, treat, reassess, and stop if residual risk cannot be made acceptable. Supports listing 'stop the activity' as a treatment option. Limits: it interprets the 2021 proposal and the 2022 Council text, not the Act as adopted and amended; it concerns providers of high-risk systems; doctrinal argument, not empirical evidence. EU law, not UK law.

items.title: Insuring AI: The Role of Insurance in Artificial Intelligence Regulation
items.publisher: Harvard Journal of Law & Technology, vol. 35 no. 2; author Anat Lior
items.quote: Exceptions and exclusions can be silent rather than affirmative
items.why: Research on insurance as a way of transferring AI risk. Argues insurance can channel safer behaviour, and sets out the drawbacks: moral hazard, difficulty pricing unfamiliar risks, and exclusions, including risks an insurer never foresaw and later writes out of standard policies. Supports the brief's caution that cover is uncertain. Limits: United States law and market; a law-review article (student-edited, not blind peer review); argument, not claims data; 2022.

items.title: Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry: Report, Volume 1 (HC 1119)
items.publisher: Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry (Sir Wyn Williams)
items.quote: the Post Office maintained the fiction that its data was always accurate
items.why: A statutory inquiry's finding on what happens when a known system risk is neither treated nor formally accepted: staff knew, or should have known, the system could produce false data, yet the organisation acted as if it could not. Limits: Horizon was an accounting system, not AI; Volume 1 deals with human impact and redress, and the inquiry's findings on governance and responsibility are for later volumes, not read here.

items.title: Model Artificial Intelligence Governance Framework, Second Edition
items.publisher: Infocomm Media Development Authority and Personal Data Protection Commission, Singapore
items.quote: mitigate those risks, and maintain a response plan should mitigation fail
items.why: International comparator. Singapore's voluntary framework treats risk treatment as continuing work: identify and review risks, mitigate them, keep a response plan in case mitigation fails, and record any departure from the organisation's own values as a conscious decision with a documented rationale. Voluntary; no legal force in the UK; predates generative AI.
